Two inferential targets, different returns to case volume: theory and evidence for epidemic reproduction numbers

Abstract

This study asks why additional reported cases sharpen an estimate of the current reproduction number but do much less for an estimate of transmission across periods. In a branching process with environmental variation, overdispersed offspring and binomial reporting, a conditionally unbiased estimate from m reported cases has mean squared error A/m about the current value Rt and vR+A/m about the mean across periods, because true variation of Rt between periods is irreducible sampling variation for the second target. Precision for that target levels off beyond the balance scale m×=A/vR. Volatile reporting adds a term independent of m. With independent periods and linear costs, a fixed budget is better spent on further periods once m exceeds (c0/c1)m×. In US influenza admissions during early growth in four seasons, an affine loss model gave an apparent balance ratio of 37.4 admissions per week (95% CI 19.1 to 71.0), and a power law fitted about as well. Binomial thinning steepened the slope at 0.41 (95% CI 0.31 to 0.53), compatible with the Poisson value of 0.45. State intercepts gave 17.3 (95% CI 3.3 to 51.4), not distinguishable from the cross-sectional value. Simulation-based calibration gave an environmental variance of 0.040 (95% CI 0.026 to 0.056) for a baseline mean generation interval of 3.6 days and 0.013 to 0.026 for 2.2 to 2.9 days. Between 41% and 51% of the intercept was shared by all states within a week, and 55% of state-weeks lay above the apparent ratio and about 44% above the latent scale.

Keywords Reproduction number; Environmental stochasticity; Surveillance design; Reporting heterogeneity; Influenza hospitalisation; Diminishing returns

1. Introduction

Estimates of the time-varying reproduction number have become a routine output of infectious disease surveillance. They were used to track the transmission of Ebola virus disease in West Africa (Nouvellet et al., 2018), to assess non-pharmaceutical interventions against COVID-19 (Flaxman et al., 2020) and to describe the early spread of SARS-CoV-2 (Kucharski et al., 2020). They are now produced routinely for many countries (Huisman et al., 2022), with practical guidance on their estimation (Gostic et al., 2020; Steyn et al., 2025). Their value for situational awareness depends on how precisely they can be estimated from the data that surveillance systems actually collect.

The instantaneous reproduction number, Rt, is the expected number of secondary infections generated by an individual infected at time t if conditions remained as they were at that time (Fraser, 2007). It is usually estimated from incidence through the renewal equation, which weights past incidence by the generation interval (Wallinga and Teunis, 2004; Cori et al., 2013; Thompson et al., 2019). The generation interval is the time between infection of a primary case and infection of its secondary cases. For a given generation interval, the posterior uncertainty of such estimates shrinks as the number of cases in the estimation window increases (Cori et al., 2013). Parag and colleagues improved estimation at low incidence (Parag, 2021). They also quantified in closed form the information that incidence carries about Rt, including the loss caused by time-varying reporting fractions (Parag et al., 2022), and derived the limits this information places on timely interventions (Parag et al., 2025). Extensions handle temporally aggregated counts (Nash et al., 2023; Ogi-Gittins et al., 2024) and the difference between the reproduction number of infections and the apparent reproduction number of a delayed observation series (Eales and Riley, 2024).

These precision results measure error against the realised value of Rt in the period being estimated, and that error vanishes as case counts grow. Many uses of Rt estimates refer instead to a quantity that persists across periods, such as the typical level of transmission in a season or the value expected next week. Policy evaluations likewise average over weeks with different climatic conditions, school calendars and contact patterns, all of which modulate influenza transmission (Cauchemez et al., 2008; Shaman and Kohn, 2009; Shaman et al., 2010). Between-period variation in Rt is shared by all chains of transmission in a population at a given time. Population ecology distinguishes such environmental stochasticity from demographic stochasticity, which arises from independent individual outcomes (Engen et al., 1998; Rohani et al., 2002; Lande et al., 2003), and mechanistic epidemic models have included both forms (Bretó et al., 2009). Demographic variance per individual falls with population size, whereas environmental variance does not, and the population size at which the two contributions are equal is a standard summary of extinction risk (Lande, 1993; Lande et al., 2003). Overdispersed offspring distributions (Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005; Endo et al., 2020) and incomplete reporting add to the demographic side of this partition.

Surveillance data add a third source of variation. The proportion of infections that appear in a count changes over time with testing practice, care seeking and the completeness of facility reporting (Azmon et al., 2014; Stoner et al., 2019; Parag and Donnelly, 2022). In the United States, hospitals were required to report influenza admissions to the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) from February 2022 (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2022; Frutos et al., 2026). Reporting was voluntary from May to October 2024 and required again from November 2024 (Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, 2024; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2026). Hospital admission series of this kind are increasingly used for forecasting and real-time assessment (Mathis et al., 2024). Variation in reporting completeness that persists within a week acts on every case in that week and therefore behaves like environmental variation, not like sampling noise.

Sample size calculations for surveillance usually assume that more cases give proportionally more precision (Cochran, 1977), and analyses of reproduction number estimation have concentrated on the informativeness of incidence for period-specific values (Parag et al., 2022; Bhatt et al., 2023). A variance that is the sum of a term shared within a unit and a term that falls with the number of observations in the unit is, however, familiar from several fields. It is the variance of a cluster mean in two-stage sampling (Cochran, 1977), and it appears in sample size calculations for cluster-randomised trials. There the between-cluster coefficient of variation sets the number of clusters needed and the cost ratio sets the optimal cluster size (Hayes and Bennett, 1999; Raudenbush, 1997). Designs for detecting trends in repeated ecological surveys face the same structure, because variation shared by all sites in a year limits what additional sites can achieve (Urquhart and Kincaid, 1999; Kincaid et al., 2004). State-space models of population dynamics show that process and observation variance are often difficult to separate from a single series (Knape, 2008; Auger-Méthé et al., 2016). Stochastic epidemic models fitted to incidence include environmental noise in transmission alongside demographic noise (Bretó et al., 2009; He et al., 2010; Dureau et al., 2013; King et al., 2015). The form vR+A/m is therefore classical. What surveillance for the reproduction number adds is the content of each term. The term that falls with case volume depends on the mean reproduction number through overdispersed offspring and binomial reporting, volatile reporting completeness adds a term that does not fall with case volume, and a budget is spread over several periods.

An empirical test also faces a measurement problem. Weekly growth statistics computed from admissions are apparent quantities whose variance depends on the delay from infection to admission and on how each statistic aggregates growth, so their intercepts cannot be read directly as transmission variance. Observations from the same calendar week share national influences, and interval estimates that treat them as independent are too narrow (Owen, 2007; Cameron et al., 2011).

The central point is a distinction between inferential targets. For the current value Rt, the error of a case-count estimate is counting error, and it vanishes as cases per period accumulate. For the mean reproduction number across periods, the true variation of Rt from one period to the next is part of the error. It is not counting error that more cases per period would remove, nor is it uninformative noise. It is irreducible sampling variation of the cross-period target, and only more periods reduce it. Our contribution is not the variance partition itself. It is a mechanistic version for case-count surveillance under negative binomial offspring and binomial reporting, the balance scale m× at which its two parts are equal, its consequences for volatile reporting and for dividing a fixed budget between cases per period and number of periods, and an empirical calibration. For the calibration we fit the relative loss of two apparent weekly statistics in NHSN influenza admissions against case volume and map their intercepts to the latent environmental variance through a data-matched simulation, keeping the apparent scale of each statistic distinct from the latent scale of the model (Table 1). Two further analyses address what a cross-sectional fit cannot: binomial thinning of the observed counts tests whether the term that falls with case volume scales as the model predicts, and state intercepts separate the cross-sectional slope from the slope within states. Finally, we decompose the intercept into national-week and state-specific components and compare the mandatory and voluntary reporting regimes.

2. Model and theory

2.1. Transmission, reporting and two estimation targets

Consider transmission over one generation, indexed by t, in which n infected individuals act as primary cases. Conditional on the instantaneous reproduction number Rt, the number of secondary infections caused by primary case i, Xi,t, is assumed to follow a negative binomial distribution, which captures individual heterogeneity in transmission (Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005). The offspring distribution is given by:

(1)

where k>0 is the dispersion parameter, smaller values of k correspond to greater heterogeneity, and k→∞ recovers Poisson offspring. Each infection is then reported independently with probability ρ∈(0,1]. Because a sum of independent negative binomial variables with a common success probability is negative binomial, and because binomial thinning preserves this family, the reported count Ct satisfies:

(2)

where m=ρn is the expected number of reported cases per period when Rt=1. We refer to m as the case volume.

The model rests on four assumptions. Each infection is reported independently with a probability ρ that does not change over time (H1). Primary cases transmit independently and identically according to Eq. (1) (H2). The dispersion k does not depend on Rt or n (H3). The number of primary cases n is fixed by design and is independent of Rt (H4). Assumption H4 holds when n is set by contact tracing; in routine surveillance n is itself the outcome of earlier transmission, and the renewal formulation in Section 3.3 relaxes it.

Two scales recur in what follows (Table 1). The quantities of the model, namely Rt, its mean R¯ and variance vR, the case volume m and the balance scale defined below, are latent and refer to one generation of transmission. The weekly statistics computed from admissions in Section 3.2, and the intercept a, slope b and ratio b/a fitted to their relative loss, are apparent quantities defined on the scale of each statistic and on weeks. The ratio b/a would equal the balance scale only if a week were a single generation and the reporting scale were free of noise (Section 3.3). We therefore call b/a the apparent balance ratio, reserve m× for the latent balance scale, and link the two through the calibration of Section 3.10.

Transmission potential varies between periods with climatic conditions, school terms and behaviour (Cauchemez et al., 2008; Shaman and Kohn, 2009; Dalziel et al., 2018). Its marginal moments are denoted 𝔼(Rt)=R¯ and Var(Rt)=vR. Because this variation acts on every chain of transmission in the same period, it corresponds to environmental stochasticity in population ecology, whereas the offspring and reporting variation of Eq. (2) corresponds to demographic stochasticity (Engen et al., 1998; Lande et al., 2003).

The scaled count R̂t=Ct/m can be used for two different targets. The first is the current value Rt, which is the quantity of interest for situational awareness and for judging whether transmission is currently above one. The second is the mean across periods, R¯, which is the quantity of interest when describing typical transmission in a season. Two related targets, the mean of the realised values over a finite set of periods and the value in the next period, are treated in Corollary 1. The error for the first target is R̂t−Rt. The error for the second target can be written as:

(3)

where the second term does not depend on m. Conditional on Rt, R̂t is unbiased for Rt, and its variance Rt/m+ρRt2/(km) falls to zero as m grows; in this case R̂t attains the Cramér–Rao bound for Rt (Appendix A). Because the first term of Eq. (3) has mean zero given Rt, the two terms are uncorrelated, and the mean squared errors of the two targets differ by exactly vR. This identity requires three conditions: the estimate is conditionally unbiased for Rt, the case volume m does not depend on Rt (H4), and ρ is fixed and known (H1). For the cross-period target, the true variation of Rt between periods is therefore part of the error; it is sampling variation of that target, not counting error, and it does not fall with m.

2.2. Error variance and the balance scale

For the second target, the error variance follows from the law of total variance applied to Eq. (3).

Proposition 1 (Error variance for the mean across periods). Under H1–H4, the mean squared error of R̂t=Ct/(ρn) about Rt is A/m, and its variance about R¯ is given by:

(4)

where the three terms are the environmental, reporting and offspring contributions. Then:

  1. for fixed ρ, V→vR as n→∞;

  2. for fixed n, V→vR+R¯/n+(R¯2+vR)/(kn)>vR as ρ→1;

  3. at the balance scale m×=A/vR, the sampling and environmental contributions are equal, and doubling m reduces V by the fraction 1/[2(1+m/m×)];

  4. among estimators that are conditionally unbiased for Rt, no estimator has a smaller mean squared error for R¯ than V.

The balance scale plays the role of the critical population size in ecological models, at which demographic and environmental contributions to the variance of population growth are equal (Lande, 1993; Lande et al., 2003). It is a reference point for comparing the two contributions and does not by itself define a minimum operating size. Part (iv) is restricted to conditionally unbiased estimators. An estimator that shrinks R̂t towards a prior mean can have smaller error for R¯ (Appendix B.5).

Parts (i) and (ii) show that case volume can be raised in two ways with different limits. Coverage n removes both sampling terms in the limit, whereas full reporting leaves the offspring term. Near the baseline, a small proportional increase in n reduces V by A/R¯ times as much as the same proportional increase in ρ.

The single-period result extends to estimates that combine several periods. Let R¯T=T−1∑t=1TRt denote the mean of the realised values over T periods, and let Rt follow either independent draws or a stationary first-order autoregressive process with autocorrelation ϕ.
